title: Picking your vertical
summary: How the money really flows in eight common verticals, how to match one to your budget, geo, skills and risk, how to read offer pages and talk to affiliate managers. You finish with a scored, written first-vertical decision and a 7-day plan.

lessons.title: What a vertical is and how its money flows
objectives: By the end you can say who pays, for what action and when, in eight common verticals.
You can name the event that triggers your payout in each vertical and why some take weeks to confirm.
You can state which verticals are regulated and what that means before you spend a single dollar.

steps.h: A vertical is a buyer, an action and a rulebook
steps.p: The How the money works module gave you the list of verticals. Now go one level deeper. Every vertical answers three questions in its own way: who pays you, which user action they pay for, and which rules decide whether that action counts. Learn those three answers and any new offer becomes easy to read.
steps.more: Beginners often pick a vertical by its payout headline. Experienced buyers pick it by its money flow. The money flow tells you how long you wait for cash, how much a single mistake costs, how many results you need before you learn anything, and how likely an ad platform is to stop you. Two offers can both say "$50 CPA" and behave completely differently: one pays on a delivered parcel after two weeks, the other pays on a verified deposit after a 30 day hold. In this lesson we walk through eight verticals and trace the money in each, so that in lesson 2 you can match one to your budget, geo and skills.

d.b: Who pays, for what, under which rules

steps.say: In the How the money works module, you met the list of verticals. Now we go one level deeper. Look at the line on screen: who pays, for what, under which rules. Every vertical answers those three questions in its own way. Beginners often pick a vertical by its payout headline. Experienced buyers pick it by its money flow, because two offers can both say fifty dollars C P A, cost per acquisition, and behave completely differently. In this lesson we trace the money in eight verticals.

steps.h: Follow the money in a trading offer
steps.p: Here is one full money flow, using a trading offer as the example. The user deposits with the broker. The broker reports the deposit to the network. The network checks it against the offer rules and pays you. You paid the ad platform days or weeks earlier.
steps.more: Notice where the delays sit. The ad platform charges you as the impressions happen. The broker only reports a first time deposit (FTD) after the user has verified identity (KYC) and funded the account, which can take days. The network then holds the conversion for a validation period to catch fraud and chargebacks, and pays on its schedule. So the cash you spent on Monday might come back as payout three to six weeks later. Every vertical has a version of this map. The steps change, but the question is always the same: at which box does the money finally reach you?
steps.say: Here's one full money flow, using a trading offer as the example. Follow the map from your ad. The click goes to a prelander, the user signs up, then passes K Y C, know your customer checks, and deposits with the broker. The broker reports the F T D, the first time deposit, to the network by postback. The network checks it against the offer rules, and pays you after a hold. Notice where the delays sit: you paid the ad platform days or weeks earlier. Money spent on Monday might come back three to six weeks later.

steps.h: How the money verticals pay
steps.p: Four verticals pay on financial actions. Payouts tend to be larger, approval checks stricter and confirmation slower. This is a rough guide; every offer page sets its own terms, so read the actual page before you trust any row here.
steps.say: Four verticals pay on financial actions. Look down the table. Trading usually pays C P A, RevShare or a hybrid, on a verified first deposit. iGaming pays the same ways, on a first deposit above a baseline. Finance and loans pay per lead or per acquisition, on a lead, an approval or a funded account. Sweepstakes pay per lead, single or double opt-in, on a valid entry. Payouts here tend to be larger, checks stricter, and confirmation slower. This is a rough guide, so read the actual offer page before you trust any row.

steps.h: How the product verticals pay
steps.p: The other four pay on purchases, installs or sign-ups. Payouts are usually smaller per result, but each result is often cheaper and faster to get, which matters a lot when your budget is small. Again, treat this as a rough guide and check each offer.
steps.say: The other verticals pay on purchases, installs or sign-ups. Look at the table. Nutra is C P A, often cash on delivery, paid when the order is approved or delivered. E-commerce pays a commission on a sale that isn't returned. Apps and utilities pay per install or in-app event. Dating pays per sign-up or paid subscription. Payouts are usually smaller per result, but each result is often cheaper and faster to get, which matters a lot when your budget is small. Again, treat this as a rough guide, and check each offer.

steps.h: Trading: paid on verified deposits
steps.p: Trading offers pay when a new user opens an account with a broker, passes identity checks and makes a first deposit. Many offers add a minimum deposit, called the baseline. Some also pay a share of what the broker earns from that user over time. Trading products are high risk and many users lose money.
steps.more: Who pays: the broker, through the network. What for: a qualified first time deposit, sometimes with extra conditions such as a number of trades. When: after the network's hold, often weekly or monthly. Brokers and their marketing are regulated in many countries, for example by a securities or financial conduct regulator. Ad platforms usually treat trading and investment as restricted financial services, which can require verification or written approval before ads run. Be careful with wording: no promises of profit, no "easy money", and a clear risk message where the law or the advertiser requires it.

steps.h: Regulated means checked before you spend
steps.p: Trading, iGaming, many finance products and some dating offers are restricted. Ads usually need platform authorization, and the advertiser usually needs a licence in the user's country. You must check the current platform policy and local law for every geo before you run. If either says no, you do not run.

steps.h: iGaming: paid on depositing players
steps.p: iGaming means online sports betting and casino. The operator pays when a new player deposits above a baseline amount, by RevShare on net gaming revenue, or both. Gambling is licensed in some countries, banned in others, and always has a legal age, usually 18 or older.
steps.more: Who pays: the licensed operator. What for: a new player who deposits at least the baseline, sometimes with a wagering condition. RevShare pays a percentage of net gaming revenue (NGR), which is what the operator keeps after winnings, bonuses and fees. When: after a hold, and RevShare monthly. In Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa gambling is regulated by national or state bodies with their own licences and ad rules; the details differ and change, so check the current position for each geo. Ad platforms usually require written permission or a certification process before gambling ads run; at the time of writing this applies on the major platforms, so check each one's current policy. Responsible gambling messages and age targeting are normal requirements, not optional extras.

d.s: Licensed operator, legal age, platform approval

steps.say: iGaming means online sports betting and casino. The licensed operator pays when a new player deposits above a baseline, or through RevShare on net gaming revenue, which is what the operator keeps after winnings, bonuses and fees, or both. Gambling is licensed in some countries, banned in others, and always has a legal age, usually eighteen or older. Ad platforms usually require written permission or certification first, so check each one's current policy. Responsible gambling messages and age targeting are normal requirements, not optional extras.

steps.h: Finance and loans: careful users, careful rules
steps.p: Finance covers loans, cards, savings, payment and banking apps. Offers pay per lead, per approved application or per funded account. Lenders are usually licensed or registered, and ads for credit often must show costs clearly. Users compare carefully, so honest, specific ads beat hype.
steps.more: Example of why the paid action matters: a loan app offer that pays $2 per completed application will get paid quickly but may push you toward volume. An offer that pays $15 per approved and disbursed loan pays only when the lender says yes, so your approval rate depends on whether you reached people who actually qualify. In several African markets digital lenders must be registered or licensed (for example with a consumer protection or central bank regulator) and some have been penalised for harsh collection practices. Before promoting a lender, check that it appears on the current official list for that country. Never write "guaranteed approval" or "no checks"; it is misleading and often illegal.
steps.say: Finance covers loans, cards, savings, payment and banking apps. Offers pay per lead, per approved application, or per funded account. Lenders are usually licensed or registered, and credit ads often must show costs clearly. Users compare carefully, so honest, specific ads beat hype. Before promoting a lender, check that it appears on the current official list for that country. And never write guaranteed approval or no checks. It's misleading and often illegal.

steps.h: Sweepstakes: honest entry or hidden charge
steps.p: Sweepstakes offers pay per entry, usually a single opt-in (SOI: one form) or a double opt-in (DOI: the user confirms by email or SMS). Leads are cheap and fast. The risk is the funnel behind the entry, which on some offers leads to subscriptions the user did not clearly agree to.

a.title: Skip offers like this
items: Prize is the only thing shown

steps.say: Sweepstakes offers pay per entry, either a single opt-in, one form, or a double opt-in, where the user confirms by email or S M S. Leads are cheap and fast. The risk is the funnel behind the entry. Compare the two sides. Skip offers where the prize is the only thing shown, with hidden S M S or carrier billing, hard-to-find terms, or you have won style ads. Run offers with a real prize and draw, clear entry terms and dates, no charge to enter, and an ad that says enter a prize draw.

steps.h: Nutra and COD: paid on approved orders
steps.p: Nutra offers in Africa often run cash on delivery (COD). The user leaves a name and phone number, a call centre confirms the order, and you are paid per approved order. Some offers only count delivered parcels. Health claims are where most nutra campaigns break the rules and the law.
steps.more: The flow: your ad, an order form, a call from the advertiser's call centre, then approval and delivery. The approval rate is the share of leads the call centre confirms. A low approval rate kills your profit even when leads look cheap. Health products are regulated: in many countries supplements cannot claim to treat, cure or prevent disease, and food and drug regulators can act against misleading ads. Platforms reject before-and-after images, weight-loss figures and "doctors hate this" style copy. If you choose nutra, choose products you can describe honestly, such as a skincare item, and leave out medical claims entirely.

steps.h: Example: what one COD lead is really worth
steps.p: This is the single most useful COD calculation. The payout only arrives on approved orders, so the value of each lead is the payout multiplied by the approval rate. That number, not the payout, is your ceiling for cost per lead. Example figures only.
steps.more: Example: a COD offer pays $10 per approved order. Of every 100 leads you send, the call centre approves 40. So 100 leads earn 40 × $10 = $400, or $4 per lead. If your ads produce leads at $3, you keep $1 per lead before any other costs. If they cost $5, you lose $1 on every lead even though $5 looks small next to a $10 payout. If an offer also requires delivery, multiply again by the delivery rate. At 80% delivery, $10 × 40% × 80% = $3.20 per lead.
steps.say: This is the single most useful C O D calculation. Read the equation: a ten dollar payout, times forty percent approval, equals four dollars per lead. The payout only arrives on approved orders, so that four dollars, not the ten, is your ceiling for cost per lead. If your leads cost three dollars, you keep one dollar each. If they cost five, you lose a dollar on every lead. And if delivery is required too, multiply again: at eighty percent delivery, it's three dollars twenty per lead. These are example figures only.

steps.h: E-commerce: a share of the sale
steps.p: E-commerce offers pay a commission per sale (CPS), either a fixed amount or a percentage of the basket. Returned or cancelled orders are removed. Legal risk is low when products are real and described honestly, which makes it a good place to learn the craft.
steps.more: Example: a shop pays 8% commission. A $50 basket earns you $4. If one sale needs about 25 clicks and clicks cost $0.10, a sale costs you $2.50 in traffic and you keep $1.50. Small numbers, but you get many results per dollar, so you learn faster. Watch for cookie windows (how long after the click a sale still counts), return periods (commission is often confirmed only after the return window closes) and banned methods such as bidding on the shop's brand name in search when the offer forbids it.

steps.h: Apps and utilities: installs and events
steps.p: App offers pay per install (CPI) or per in-app event such as registration, first top-up or subscription. Payouts are small. Apps are usually not heavily regulated unless they handle money, health or gambling. Fraud checks are strict: fake or bot installs are found and removed.
steps.more: Many app offers have moved from pure installs to events, because installs alone are easy to fake. An example offer might pay $0.40 per install in one geo or $3 per completed registration. Store rules also matter: the app store, not just the ad platform, has policies on how apps may be promoted. If the app is a wallet, loan app or betting app, it is a finance or iGaming offer wearing app clothes, and all the rules of that vertical apply.

Apps aren't usually heavily regulated, unless they handle money, health or gambling. Fraud checks are strict, so fake or bot installs are found and removed. And here's a key point: if the app is a wallet, loan app or betting app, it's a finance or iGaming offer wearing app clothes, and all the rules of that vertical apply.

steps.h: Dating: sign-ups and subscriptions
steps.p: Dating offers pay per sign-up (SOI or DOI) or per paid subscription. Many ad platforms restrict dating ads and may need prior approval. Adult content is banned on mainstream platforms at the time of writing; check each platform's current policy. Fake profiles, sexualised images and misleading "matches near you" claims break policy and trust.
steps.more: Dating is often sold to beginners as easy, cheap leads. The reality: mainstream platforms usually list dating as restricted and ask the advertiser to be approved, and adult dating is usually not allowed at all. Offers must target adults only. Ads with stock photos implying a real person is waiting for the user are misleading. If you consider dating, start with the platform policy page for dating ads and the offer's own allowed traffic list, and confirm both before writing a single ad.

steps.h: Five questions for any vertical
steps.p: Before you spend time on a vertical, answer these five in writing. If you cannot answer one, ask the network or read further. You will use these answers in lesson 2 to match a vertical to your own situation.

Which user action triggers my payout?
How long until that payout is cash?
Which regulator and platform rules apply?
What will make a result get rejected?

takeaways: A vertical is defined by who pays, which action they pay for and the rules that decide if it counts.
The real value of a result is the payout times the approval rate, not the payout headline.
Trading, iGaming, many finance offers and dating are restricted: check advertiser licence, platform authorization and local law for each geo.
Faster, smaller payouts (apps, e-commerce, honest lead gen) give more results per dollar and faster learning.

glossary.def: The path from your ad spend to the payout reaching you, including who pays, for which action and after which delays.
Single opt-in. A lead that counts after one form submission.
Double opt-in. A lead that counts only after the user confirms, usually by clicking an email link or entering an SMS code.
The share of your leads or orders the advertiser confirms as valid. Payout times approval rate is the true value per lead.
Cost per sale. You are paid a fixed amount or a percentage of each completed sale.
Net gaming revenue. What a gambling operator keeps after player winnings, bonuses and fees; the base for iGaming RevShare.

quiz.q: A COD offer pays $12 per approved order. The call centre approves 25% of your leads. What is each lead worth to you?
quiz.why: $12 × 25% = $3. Only approved orders pay, so a lead is worth the payout times the approval rate.

quiz.q: Which statement about a trading offer's money flow is accurate?
options: You are paid when the user clicks your ad
You are paid when the user registers, before any checks
You are paid by the ad platform
You are usually paid after a verified first deposit and a hold period
quiz.why: Trading offers usually pay on a qualified first deposit after KYC, and networks hold conversions before paying.

quiz.q: A sweepstakes offer's funnel leads to an SMS subscription the user is not clearly told about. What should you do?
options: Skip it
Run it but use softer ad wording
Run it only on cheap traffic
Run it and hide the terms on a second page
quiz.why: A hidden charge misleads users. No wording fixes the offer itself, so you skip it.

quiz.q: Before running an iGaming offer in a new country, which check is required?
options: Only that the payout is above $50
That your friends like the brand
That the operator is licensed there, the platform has authorised the ads and local ad law allows it
Only that the network accepts the geo
quiz.why: Gambling is regulated. You need the advertiser licence, platform authorization and local law to all say yes before you run.

quiz.q: Why do e-commerce and app offers suit learning, despite small payouts?
options: They pay more per result
They give more results per dollar, so you get feedback faster
They have no rules at all
They never reject conversions
quiz.why: Cheaper results mean more data points from the same budget, so you learn which ads work sooner. They still have rules and rejections.

lessons.title: Matching a vertical to your budget, geo, skills and risk
objectives: By the end you can work out how many test results your budget can actually buy in each vertical.
You can filter verticals by what is legal and practical in your geo, and by the skills you already have.
You can use the vertical picker and explain its suggestions with your own numbers.

steps.h: Fit beats payout
steps.p: The best vertical for you is not the one with the biggest numbers in someone else's screenshot. It is the one where your budget buys enough results to learn, your geo allows the offer, your skills make good ads, and a bad week does not end your career.
steps.say: Here's the big idea of this lesson: fit beats payout. The best vertical for you isn't the one with the biggest numbers in someone else's screenshot. It's the one where your budget buys enough results to learn, your geo allows the offer, your skills make good ads, and a bad week doesn't end your career. Look at the screen: your vertical, not theirs. Budget, geo, skills and risk.

steps.p: Run every vertical through four filters in this order. Budget and geo remove options fast. Skills and risk then choose between what is left. A vertical must pass all four, so one hard no is enough to drop it for now.

Geo|is it legal and practical where you target?
Skills|can you make honest ads for it?
Risk|can you survive holds, bans and losses?

steps.h: Rough guide: the minimum test budget
steps.p: You cannot judge an offer from one result. A common rough guide is to plan for at least three to five times your target cost per result as a test budget for one offer. It varies by geo and vertical, but it stops you from testing with money that only buys luck.
steps.more: Why three to five? With zero or one result you cannot tell a bad offer from bad luck. A few results at or near your target tell you whether the numbers are in reach. Example: if your target CPA is $40, plan $120 to $200 for one test. If you have $300 in total, that means one or two real tests, not ten. This is why budget is the first filter: a $300 budget simply cannot test a vertical where one result costs $80 to $150, however good the payout looks.
steps.say: You can't judge an offer from one result. Read the equation: target C P A, cost per acquisition, times three to five, equals your test budget per offer. That's a common rough guide, and it varies by geo and vertical. For example, with a forty dollar target, plan one hundred and twenty to two hundred dollars for one test. If you have three hundred dollars in total, that's one or two real tests, not ten. It stops you testing with money that only buys luck.

steps.h: Starting rules for a test budget
steps.p: Example: target CPA $40, payout $50. Kill an ad set at $80 spend with 0 conversions. From $120 spend, kill it if CPA is above $50, the lower of $60 and break-even. Scale +20% at most every 48 hours at CPA $32 or less with 3+ conversions.
steps.more: These are starting rules, the same ones taught in the Budget and kill rules module, worked out for a $40 target. 2 × $40 = $80 is the zero-conversion kill line. 3 × $40 = $120 is the point where CPA is judged. 1.5 × $40 = $60, but the $50 payout is lower, so $50 is the CPA kill line. 0.8 × $40 = $32 is the scale line, and it needs at least 3 network-confirmed conversions. Notice what this means for budget: a test that cannot reach $120 on one ad set can only ever trigger the first rule. Adapt the rules as you gain data.

steps.h: Geo: legal first, then practical
steps.p: For every geo ask, in order: is this vertical legal here, can ads for it run here on my traffic source, and can users here actually pay or sign up? Payment methods, language, device type and data costs all change what works.
steps.more: Example: a trading offer may accept Nigeria on the network page, but you still need the broker to be allowed to serve Nigerian clients, the ad platform to allow the ads for that country and your copy to meet local rules. Then the practical layer: if the offer requires card deposits but most of your audience pays with bank transfer or mobile money, conversion rates drop. If the landing page is only in English and you target Francophone Cameroon, expect poor results. Write these checks down per geo; they rarely change week to week, so you do it once.

steps.h: Effective payout: the number that matters
steps.p: Not every result you send is approved. If past offers or the manager tell you roughly 70% of FTDs end up qualified, the effective payout is lower than the headline. Plan with the effective number, not the advertised one. Example figures only.

If you had planned your bids around $80, you would have been losing money while thinking you were profitable. Ask the affiliate manager what a typical qualification rate looks like for new affiliates in your geo, and treat the answer as a guide, not a promise.

The advertiser logo

lessons.title: Talking to your affiliate manager
objectives: By the end you can write a first message that gets a useful reply instead of a template.
You can list the questions to ask before you run any offer, and get the answers in writing.
You can ask for a better payout or a test agreement using numbers, and recognise advice you must refuse.

steps.h: A partner, not a vending machine
steps.p: Your affiliate manager (AM) looks after many affiliates and is judged on the quality and volume they bring. Help them see you as someone who will send real users and follow the rules, and you get better answers, offers and terms.
steps.more: Managers receive a flood of messages that say "hi bro, best offer?" with nothing else. Those get a link and nothing more. A message that says who you are, which geo and source you plan to use, your budget and what you need to know tells the manager you are serious. It also lets them protect you: a good manager will warn you that a source is banned on an offer, or that a geo has a low qualification rate, before you lose money finding out.

d.b: Be the affiliate they want to help

steps.say: Your affiliate manager, or A M, looks after many affiliates, and is judged on the quality and volume they bring. As the screen says, be the affiliate they want to help: clear, honest, specific and patient. Managers get a flood of messages saying hi bro, best offer, and those get a link and nothing more. A message that says who you are, your geo, source and budget tells them you're serious, and lets them warn you about problems before you lose money.

steps.h: A first message that gets a real reply
steps.p: Here is an example first chat with a manager on a network. The affiliate is clear and honest about being new. Notice that the manager answers with specifics, because the question was specific.

messages.text: Hi Ada, I am Tobi, new affiliate from Lagos. Approved yesterday. I plan to test COD e-commerce in Nigeria with Meta traffic, about $250 test budget.
Which 2 or 3 COD offers have the best approval rates for new affiliates in NG right now?
Welcome Tobi. For NG COD on Meta, look at #2210 (kitchen set) and #2231 (phone accessories). Approval has been around 40 to 50% recently. Don't use health claims; those get rejected.
Thanks. Is a prelander allowed on both, or direct to the order form only?
Both allow prelanders. Send me the link before you launch and I will check it.

steps.say: Here's an example first chat with a manager. Look at Tobi's messages. He says who he is, that he's new, and that he's approved. He names his plan: C O D e-commerce, cash on delivery, in Nigeria, with Meta traffic, and about two hundred and fifty dollars to test. Then he asks one specific question. Notice how the manager answers with specifics: two offer numbers, recent approval rates, and a warning about health claims. A specific question gets a specific answer.

steps.h: Common mistakes in messages to managers
steps.p: The difference is not politeness. It is information. The manager can only help with what you tell them. A good message also shows you have already read the offer page, so you are not asking what is written there.

a.title: Gets ignored
items: Demands a higher payout on day one

steps.say: The difference between these columns isn't politeness. It's information. On the left, messages that get ignored: hi bro, best offer, no geo or source, asking what the page already says, and demanding a higher payout on day one. On the right, messages that get answered: name, geo, source and budget, one or two specific questions, showing you've read the terms, and asking for advice, not favours. The manager can only help with what you tell them.

steps.h: Ask these before you run
steps.p: Get these answers in writing before you spend. Some are on the offer page but are worth confirming, because pages are not always up to date. Save the chat; if there is a dispute later, written answers protect you.
d: Is my traffic source allowed on this offer?
Is my geo active and is the cap open?
What is a typical approval or qualification rate?
Can you check my prelander and ads first?
When exactly will I be paid?
How do I see rejected results and why?
steps.say: Get these answers in writing before you spend. Is my traffic source allowed on this offer? Is my geo active, and is the cap open? What's a typical approval or qualification rate? Can you check my prelander and ads first? When exactly will I be paid? And how do I see rejected results, and why? Some of this is on the offer page, but confirm it, because pages aren't always up to date. Save the chat. If there's a dispute later, written answers protect you.

steps.h: Asking about KPIs and holds
steps.p: This example chat shows an affiliate clarifying a trading offer before applying. The manager confirms the authorization requirement directly. If a manager ever says the opposite, that is a problem with the manager, not a loophole.

messages.text: Hi Musa. On offer #1042, the KPI says 30% of FTDs must make 5+ trades in 14 days. If I miss it, is the whole batch rejected or only the shortfall?
We review per week. If you are below 30% we usually adjust the payout for that week, not reject everything. Repeated misses can pause your access.
Clear. And for Meta, the page says social with authorization. Does the broker hold a licence for NG, and do I need my own ad authorization?
Yes, the broker is licensed for the geos listed. You need to meet Meta's financial ads rules and authorization for your account and country. No authorization, no Meta traffic.

steps.say: This example chat shows an affiliate clarifying a trading offer before applying. First, he asks about the K P I, the key performance indicator: if he misses it, is the whole batch rejected? The manager explains it's reviewed per week. Then he asks about Meta. Look at the manager's last reply: the broker is licensed for the listed geos, and the affiliate needs Meta's financial ads authorization. No authorization, no Meta traffic. If a manager ever says the opposite, that's a problem with the manager, not a loophole.

steps.h: What you can negotiate, and when
steps.p: As a new affiliate you can negotiate less than you think. After you have sent consistent, quality results, much more opens up. Rough guide only; every network has its own policy.
steps.say: As a new affiliate, you can negotiate less than you think. Look at the two columns. As a beginner, payout changes are rare, you get a small test cap, standard payment terms, and no private offers. But you can ask for a creative or page review. After proven quality, payouts often move with data, caps rise step by step, payment can be faster or weekly, and private offers sometimes open up. This is a rough guide, and every network has its own policy.

steps.h: Earn a raise with data, not pressure
steps.p: Payout increases come from results the advertiser likes: steady volume, high qualification rates, low fraud and few complaints. Bring those numbers and ask clearly. Threatening to leave for a network you have never tested rarely works.
steps.say: So how do you earn a better payout? With data, not pressure. Look at the screen: quality first, then the ask. Payout increases come from results the advertiser likes: steady volume, high qualification rates, low fraud and few complaints. Bring those numbers and ask clearly. Threatening to leave for a network you've never tested rarely works.

steps.h: Negotiating a payout bump
steps.p: Example of a payout request done well, after four weeks of results. The affiliate leads with data, makes a specific ask and offers something in return. The manager gives a partial yes with a condition, which is normal.

messages.text: Hi Ada. Last 4 weeks on #2231: 212 orders, 51% approved, no fraud flags. Daily volume has been steady at 7 to 9 approved.
Could you move me from $6 to $7 per approved order? With that I can push to 12 to 15 a day.
Good numbers. I can do $6.50 now, and $7 if you hold above 45% approval at 12+ a day for two weeks.
Deal. Please confirm the new rate on the offer page so my reports match.

steps.say: Here's a payout request done well, after four weeks of results. Read the affiliate's first message: two hundred and twelve orders, fifty one percent approved, no fraud flags, steady daily volume. Then a specific ask: move from six dollars to seven, and in return push volume higher. The manager gives a partial yes, six fifty now, and seven if approval holds above forty five percent at twelve or more a day for two weeks. That's normal. And notice the last message: confirm the new rate on the offer page, so reports match.

steps.h: Example: what a small bump is worth
steps.p: A payout increase looks small per result. Multiply it by your volume to see what it is worth over a month. This also tells you how much effort a negotiation deserves. Example figures only.
steps.more: Example: at 10 approved orders a day for 30 days you have 300 orders. A $0.50 increase adds $150 a month with no extra ad spend. At 3 orders a day, the same bump is worth $45, which is why managers say no to beginners: the difference is too small to justify for the advertiser, and too small to be worth much to you. Focus on approval rate first; raising approval from 40% to 50% on the same leads often beats any payout bump.
steps.say: A payout bump looks small per result. Read the equation: plus fifty cents per order, times three hundred orders a month, equals plus one hundred and fifty dollars a month, with no extra ad spend. But at three orders a day, the same bump is worth only forty five dollars. That's why managers say no to beginners. So focus on approval rate first. Raising approval from forty to fifty percent on the same leads often beats any payout bump. These are example figures.

steps.h: Agreeing a test before you scale
steps.p: Some managers will agree a test: a small cap, a clear time frame and the numbers that decide what happens next. Write it down in chat. It sets expectations on both sides and protects you if results are questioned later.

messages.text: Could we agree a 7 day test on #1042 for KE: cap 3 FTD a day, and you share qualification rate after day 7?
Yes. Cap 3/day for 7 days. I will send the KPI report on day 8. If quality is good we raise to 6/day.
Perfect. I will send creatives and the prelander for review before launch.

steps.say: Some managers will agree a test. In this example chat, the affiliate proposes a seven day test on one offer in Kenya, with a cap of three F T Ds, first time deposits, a day, and asks the manager to share the qualification rate after day seven. The manager agrees, and says that if quality is good, the cap goes to six a day. Write tests like this down in chat. It sets expectations on both sides, and protects you if results are questioned later.

steps.h: Put your rule card into the test agreement
steps.p: Example: target CPA $30 on a $40 payout. Tell the manager your rules in the same chat. Kill an ad set at $60 with 0 FTDs. From $90 spend, kill above $40 CPA. Scale +20% at most every 48 hours at $24 or less with 3+ network-confirmed FTDs.
steps.more: Sharing your rules does two things. The manager knows when you will ask for a cap increase, because your scale rule says so. And if the network's numbers arrive late, you can agree when the confirmed count for each day is final. These are starting rules; the full set is in the Budget and kill rules module.

d.text: Target $30: kill at $60 with 0. From $90, kill above $40. Scale at ≤ $24 with 3+ FTDs.

steps.say: You can put your rule card into the test agreement. In this example, the target C P A, cost per acquisition, is thirty dollars on a forty dollar payout. Tell the manager your rules in the same chat. Kill an ad set at sixty dollars with zero F T Ds. From ninety dollars of spend, kill above forty dollars C P A. Scale by twenty percent, at most every forty eight hours, at twenty four dollars or less with three or more network-confirmed F T Ds. Then the manager knows when you'll ask for a cap increase. These are starting rules.

steps.h: Advice you must refuse
steps.p: Sometimes a manager, a "mentor" or a group admin suggests breaking a rule. This example shows how to say no politely. Advice to hide a landing page from reviewers or ignore a restriction puts your accounts and your payouts at risk, whoever suggests it.

messages.text: Just run it without authorization, use a cloaker so the reviewer sees a cooking page. Everyone does it.
No thanks. That breaks platform rules and the offer terms. I will only run where I am authorised.
Your loss.
Understood. Please send the written terms for the offer anyway; I will review them.

steps.say: Sometimes a manager, a mentor or a group admin suggests breaking a rule. In this example chat, an unknown rep says to run without authorization and use a cloaker, so the reviewer sees a cooking page. Look at the reply: no thanks, that breaks platform rules and the offer terms, I'll only run where I'm authorised. Then the affiliate still asks for the written terms. Advice like this puts your accounts and payouts at risk, whoever suggests it.

steps.h: A manager's OK is not authorization
steps.p: A manager can tell you what the offer allows. Only the ad platform can authorize your ads, and only local law decides what is legal in a geo. If a manager says a rule does not apply, get the platform's answer yourself before you run.
steps.more: Full detail: Compliance for finance, trading and gambling offers module.

d.text: Get rules in writing, and check platform policy and local law yourself. A chat message is not permission.

If a manager says a rule doesn't apply, get the platform's answer yourself before you run. As the warning says, get rules in writing, and check platform policy and local law yourself. A chat message is not permission.

steps.h: A weekly rhythm with your manager
steps.p: Short, regular contact beats long silences and sudden demands. Once a week is enough for most beginners. Each message should carry your numbers and one clear question or update.
steps.say: Short, regular contact beats long silences and sudden demands. Follow this weekly rhythm. Send your weekly numbers. Ask about rejections. Share next week's plan. Agree any cap change. And save the chat. Once a week is enough for most beginners. Each message should carry your numbers and one clear question or update.

steps.h: Before you hit send
steps.p: A quick check for any message to a manager. It takes ten seconds and saves days of back and forth. If any answer is no, fix the message before you send it.
d: Did I give geo, source and offer ID?
Did I include numbers if I am asking for something?
Is anything I am asking for against the rules?

lessons.title: Your first-vertical decision
objectives: By the end you can score candidate verticals on a simple weighted sheet, with legal fit as a gate.
You can follow a full worked decision for a Lagos beginner with $300 and adapt it to your own numbers.
You can write a one-page decision card and a 7-day plan, then commit to it.

steps.h: Decide on paper, then commit
steps.p: You now know how verticals pay, how to check fit, how to read offers and how to talk to managers. The last step is a decision you write down, score honestly and then stick with long enough to learn from. A written decision is harder to abandon on a bad day.
steps.say: You now know how verticals pay, how to check fit, how to read offers and how to talk to managers. The last step is a decision. steps.h: The scoring sheet
steps.p: Score each candidate vertical from 1 to 5 on these criteria, multiply by the weight and add up. Legal and platform fit is not scored: it is a gate. A vertical that fails the gate is not on the sheet at all.
steps.more: Why these weights? Budget fit carries the most weight because without enough results you learn nothing, whatever else is true. Feedback speed and cash speed matter almost as much for a beginner: slow feedback means slow learning, and slow cash means your budget runs out while you wait. Skill fit decides how good your ads will be. Honest angle matters for everyone, but by the time a vertical reaches this sheet it has already passed the legal gate, so here it measures how easy it is to write a clear, truthful ad. Maximum total: 5 × (3+2+2+2+1) = 50.
steps.say: Here's the scoring sheet. Score each candidate from one to five on each criterion, multiply by the weight, and add up. Look down the table. Budget fit has the biggest weight, times three, because without enough results you learn nothing. Feedback speed, cash speed and skill fit are times two. Honest ad angle is times one. The maximum total is fifty. And notice the first row: legal and platform fit isn't scored at all. It's a gate. A vertical that fails it isn't on the sheet.

steps.h: Legal fit is a gate, not a score
steps.p: Never let a high score on budget or payout make up for a failed legal check. If the vertical needs authorization you do not have, or the product is not legal in your geo, it does not go on the sheet. Put it on a "later" list with what would need to change.

d.text: No authorization, no licence, or not legal in your geo: the vertical is out, whatever it scores elsewhere.

steps.h: Worked example: Tobi in Lagos, $300
steps.p: Tobi is a fictional beginner in Lagos. He has $300 spare, makes decent phone videos, speaks English and Pidgin, has no ad authorization for financial or gambling ads and can wait about two weeks for money. Let us score his options.
steps.more: Tobi's candidate list starts with six verticals. The gate removes three at once. Trading and iGaming usually need platform authorization and an advertiser licensed for Nigeria, and he has no authorization yet. Dating is restricted on his traffic source and he has no approved advertiser. Loans pass the legal gate only for registered lenders, and the offers his network has for Nigeria are lenders he cannot verify on the current official list, so he leaves them out too. That leaves three: COD e-commerce (non-health physical products), app installs and registrations, and an honest sweepstakes SOI offer.

steps.p: This is Tobi's one-page decision card, as an example. Every field is filled before launch. The highlighted field, the kill rules, is the one beginners most often leave empty, and it is the one that saves the most money.

blocks.label: Kill rules (target $5.60)
blocks.value: Kill at $11.20 spend with 0 approved. From $16.80 spend, kill if CPA is over $7

blocks.label: Scale rule
blocks.value: +20% at most every 48 h at CPA ≤ $4.48 with 3+ approved

blocks.label: Switch rule
blocks.value: After 30 days and 2 products, move to app registrations

steps.more: How Tobi got the numbers: target $5.60. Zero-conversion kill: 2 × $5.60 = $11.20. CPA kill applies from 3 × $5.60 = $16.80 of spend, at the lower of 1.5 × $5.60 = $8.40 and his $7 break-even, so $7. Scale: 0.8 × $5.60 = $4.48 with at least 3 approved orders. Starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module; COD approvals arrive a day or more late, so he judges only spend whose leads the call centre has finished checking.

steps.h: Tobi's 7-day plan
steps.p: A first week does not start with spending. It starts with setup, reading and checking. Tap through Tobi's plan day by day. Your days can differ; what matters is that tracking and permissions are checked before money goes out.

steps.title: Day 1: Network and offer
steps.text: Apply to one network, read two COD offers line by line and note geos, approval rates, caps and restrictions.

blocks.value: Example figures. Approval rates are recent averages, not promises.

steps.title: Day 2: Talk to the manager
steps.text: Send the first message with geo, source, budget and two questions. Ask for a creative and page check.

messages.text: Hi Ada, Tobi from Lagos. Testing #2231 on Meta, $240 over 8 days. Can you check my video and order page before launch?
Yes, send them over. No health claims and show the real price.

steps.title: Day 3: Make three videos
steps.text: Film three short videos of the real product: one demo, one unboxing, one problem and solution. Real price and COD stated.

page.p: Example only. Pay on delivery. Lagos 1 to 3 days. Price shown at checkout before you confirm.

steps.title: Day 4: Tracking check
steps.text: Build the tracking link with sub IDs, place one test order with the manager's agreement and confirm it appears in the network stats.

blocks.value: If the test does not appear, fix tracking before you spend.

steps.title: Day 5: Launch
steps.text: Launch one campaign, three ads, $30 a day. Check policy approval of each ad. Do not touch anything for 24 hours.

blocks.value: Names change; check the current Ads Manager.

steps.title: Day 6: Read the data
steps.text: Compare leads by ad, then ask the manager for approval numbers. Apply the rules only to spend whose leads have been checked: $11.20+ with 0 approved is a kill.

blocks.value: Unboxing: $11 spent, 0 approved, just under the $11.20 line. Hold one more day.

steps.title: Day 7: Write the review
steps.text: Write what you learned in five lines: best ad, cost per approved order, approval rate, problems, next test. Keep spending to day 8 as planned.

blocks.label: Cost per approved order
blocks.value: $8.75 so far, many leads still pending (example)

Day two: send the manager a first message, and ask for a creative and page check. Day three: film three short videos of the real product, with the real price and C O D stated. Day four: build the tracking link and confirm a test order appears. Day five: launch one campaign, three ads, thirty dollars a day, and don't touch it for twenty four hours. Day six: read the data, applying rules only to checked leads. Day seven: write a five-line review.

steps.h: Try it: day 8 for the unboxing ad
steps.p: On day 8, its fourth day live (launch was day 5), the unboxing ad set has spent $14 and the call centre has checked all its leads: 0 approved orders. Tobi's target is $5.60 per approved order. Apply the starting rules and make the call.
steps.more: $14 ÷ $5.60 = 2.5 times the target, with no approved orders. That is past the 2 × target zero-conversion line of $11.20, so the rule says kill. He does not restart it; a new hook goes in as a new ad set.

Compare the spend with the zero-conversion line on his decision card. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: When to switch and when to stay
steps.p: A written switch rule protects you from two mistakes: quitting a good vertical after one bad day, and holding on to a dead one for months. Switch for structural reasons, not for feelings.

b.title: Reasons to switch
items: Switch rule met after full test

steps.say: A written switch rule protects you from two mistakes: quitting a good vertical after one bad day, and holding on to a dead one for months. Compare the columns. Reasons to stay: a few bad days, one ad failed, someone else posted bigger numbers, approval dipped once. Reasons to switch: your switch rule was met after a full test, law or platform policy changed, offers were paused with no replacement, or the network isn't paying. Switch for structural reasons, not for feelings.

steps.h: Common decision mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: The decision card exists to stop these. Each mistake feels sensible on a bad day. Writing the rule before launch is what makes the right choice easy when it matters.
d: Deciding in your head|write the card before spending
No kill rule|2 × target with 0 conversions
Using the planning cost as the target|rules use payout minus margin
Judging leads not yet checked|wait for the call centre count
Switching after a bad week|follow the written switch rule
steps.say: The decision card exists to stop these mistakes. Look at the cards. Deciding in your head: write the card before spending. No kill rule: kill at two times target with zero conversions. Using the planning cost as the target: your rules use payout minus margin. Judging leads not yet checked: wait for the call centre count. Switching after a bad week: follow the written switch rule. Each mistake feels sensible on a bad day.

steps.h: Your commitment rules
steps.p: Copy these into your decision card. They turn a choice into a habit. Thirty days is long enough to see a pattern and short enough that a wrong choice does not cost you a year.
d: Stay with this vertical for 30 days
Spend only from the test budget
steps.say: Copy these commitment rules into your decision card. Stay with this vertical for thirty days. Spend only from the test budget. Log every day's numbers. Follow kill rules without arguing. And review every Sunday, in writing. They turn a choice into a habit. Thirty days is long enough to see a pattern, and short enough that a wrong choice doesn't cost you a year.

steps.h: Regulated verticals stay on the later list
steps.p: If your top score is trading, iGaming, dating or a lender, check the gate again before you write the card. Ads usually need platform authorization and the advertiser needs a licence in your geo, and local law must allow it. If any answer is no, pick the next vertical.

glossary.def: A table where you rate candidate verticals on weighted criteria to make a written, comparable decision.
A pass or fail check, such as legal and platform fit, that removes an option no matter how well it scores elsewhere.

quiz.q: A vertical scores 46/50 on your sheet, but you have no ad authorization it requires. What do you do?
options: Run it anyway because the score is high
Remove it from the sheet and put it on a "later" list
Lower its score a little
Run it on a small budget
quiz.why: Legal and platform fit is a gate. A failed gate removes the vertical whatever it scores elsewhere.

quiz.q: You want 30 approved orders at a $8 target CPA over 10 days. What daily budget does that need?
quiz.why: 30 × $8 = $240 total, ÷ 10 days = $24 a day.

quiz.q: Two verticals finish within two points of each other. What is the sensible tie-breaker?
options: The higher headline payout
The one a friend is running
The one that uses your strongest skill
Flip a coin each week
quiz.why: Skill is the hardest input to buy. Using your strongest skill usually produces better ads and faster learning.

quiz.q: Which is a good reason to switch vertical?
options: Your pre-written switch rule was met after the full test
You had two bad days
Someone posted bigger results
One ad was rejected
quiz.why: Switch for structural reasons written in advance, not short-term noise or envy.

quiz.q: What should happen on the days before your first spend?
options: Nothing; just launch
Buy followers
Read offers, message the manager, make creatives and test tracking
Apply to ten networks at once
quiz.why: Setup and a tracking test before spend prevent paying for clicks you cannot measure or offers you cannot run.

exam.q: Your spare budget is $250. You are choosing between a trading offer (about $70 per FTD, needs ad authorization you do not have) and an e-commerce offer (about $4 per sale). What is the sound first choice?
options: Trading, because one FTD pays more than many sales
E-commerce: it passes the legal gate and $250 buys enough results to learn
Both at once, $125 each
Trading, using a friend's authorised ad account
exam.why: Trading fails the gate (no authorization) and $250 buys under 4 FTDs. E-commerce gives about 60 results, enough to learn.

exam.q: A COD offer pays $9 per approved order. Approval is 35% and the offer also requires delivery, which runs at 80%. Your leads cost $3. What happens?
options: You lose about $0.48 per lead
You profit $6 per lead
You break even exactly
You profit $0.15 per lead
exam.why: $9 × 35% × 80% = $2.52 per lead. At $3 per lead you lose about $0.48 on each one.

exam.q: Offer A: $90 per FTD, about 50% qualify, paid monthly after a 30 day hold. Offer B: $60 per FTD, about 85% qualify, paid weekly. With a small budget, which is better and why?
options: A, because $90 is higher
They are identical
B: higher effective payout ($51 vs $45) and faster cash
A, because monthly payment is safer
exam.why: A = $90 × 50% = $45. B = $60 × 85% = $51, and weekly payment recycles a small budget faster.

exam.q: An offer pays $50 per FTD. 20% of registrations deposit. You want a 30% margin. Your registrations currently cost $8. What should you conclude?
options: You are profitable with room to spare
You are above your max of $7 per registration, so you are giving up margin
You need a 50% margin instead
Nothing until you have 100 FTDs
exam.why: Break-even is $50 × 20% = $10; with 30% margin the max is $7. At $8 you are still under break-even but below your target margin.

exam.q: A rep tells you a sportsbook offer works great in Ghana and you "do not need to worry about authorization, just use a cloaker". What is the right response?
options: Test it with a small budget
Use a different traffic source that does not check
Ask for a higher payout to cover the risk
Refuse; check the operator licence, platform authorization and local law yourself
exam.why: Gambling ads need a licensed operator, platform permission and compliance with local law. Cloaking is circumvention and is never acceptable.

exam.q: Payout $7 per approved COD order, 20% margin, so target $5.60. An ad set has spent $12 and the call centre has checked all its leads: 0 approved. What do the starting rules say?
options: Hold until it reaches $16.80
Kill: spend is past 2 × target ($11.20) with 0 conversions
Scale, because leads are coming in
Lower the target to $4
exam.why: 2 × $5.60 = $11.20. At $12 with 0 approved orders and no leads still pending, the zero-conversion kill applies. Leads that never get approved do not count.

exam.q: After 4 weeks you send about 240 approved orders a month at 52% approval. You ask for +$0.75 per order. What is that worth monthly, and how should you ask?
options: $75; threaten to leave
$180; lead with your volume and approval data and offer more volume
$240; ask on day one
$0.75; it is not worth asking
exam.why: 240 × $0.75 = $180 a month. Managers respond to proven quality, so lead with data and offer something in return.

exam.q: An offer page lists: payout $500 per registration, all countries, any traffic, "100% approval", minimum withdrawal $5,000, no terms. How many red flags is that?
options: None; it is generous
One: the high payout
Two
Several; walk away
exam.why: Unrealistic payout, no geos, anything allowed, guaranteed approval, a huge withdrawal minimum and no terms are each red flags. Together they point to a scam.

exam.q: Your scoring sheet totals: apps 41, COD 39, sweepstakes 34. Your strongest skill is product videos, which suits COD. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Apps, because 41 is the top score
Sweepstakes, because leads are cheapest
COD is reasonable: the scores are close and it uses your strongest skill
Run all three to see
exam.why: When totals are within a few points, skill fit is the best tie-breaker. Running all three splits a small budget too thin.

exam.q: You want 20 approved results at a $12 target CPA over 6 days, and you have $300 spare. What daily budget is needed, and what remains for reserve?
options: $40 a day, $60 reserve
$50 a day, nothing left
$20 a day, $180 reserve
$60 a day, $0 reserve
exam.why: 20 × $12 = $240, ÷ 6 days = $40 a day. $300 − $240 leaves $60 in reserve.
